opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we went back and forth on a lot. The tempting answer is to let the model decide everything: give it a "spawn subagent" tool and trust it to figure out when to fan out. Sometimes that works great. But in practice, you get two failure modes. Either the model under-delegates and tries to cram everything into one giant context, or it over-delegates and spins up a swarm of subagents for something that needed one careful pass. Both are expensive, in tokens and in quality.

The way I think about it is splitting *policy* from *judgment*. The harness should own the policy: budgets, how deep the recursion can go, what context a subagent inherits, what tools it gets, and how results come back and get merged. Those are system concerns. They're about resource management and isolation, and you want them predictable and debuggable. You don't want a model improvising its own concurrency limits.

The model should own the judgment: "This task decomposes into independent pieces," or "I need a clean context to explore this without polluting my main thread." The model actually has better information about that than any static rule we could write.

So the harness gives the model a well-shaped affordance with guardrails, and the model decides when to reach for it. One thing that helped a lot was making the cost of spawning visible to the model, so it reasons about the tradeoff instead of treating subagents as free.

The other piece is the return path. A lot of the value of a subagent is that it compresses its work into something small and useful for the parent. If the harness doesn't enforce a clear contract for what comes back, you lose most of the benefit. So honestly, I'd say the boundaries matter more than the spawn decision itself: what goes in, what comes out, and who's accountable for the result.

r001.rationale: The response assigns spawning policy to the harness, but does not locate it specifically in the harness’s executive.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we went back and forth on a lot. The naive version is you put the spawning logic in the harness. You have some orchestrator layer that looks at the task, decides it's big, and fans it out. And that feels clean from an engineering standpoint because the harness is deterministic, you can test it, you can reason about it.

But in practice it fights the model. The model has way more context about what the task actually requires than any heuristic we could write. It knows when it's hit a point where there are three independent threads worth pulling on, and it knows when something that looks parallelizable actually isn't because step two depends on what you learn in step one. So in Exo we ended up pushing that decision down into the model. Spawning a subagent is just a tool. The model calls it the same way it would call a file read or a shell command.

What the harness does own is the constraints around that. Budget, depth limits, what context gets handed to the child, how results come back. Those are the guardrails, and I think those genuinely belong in the harness because they're about system safety and cost, not about task understanding. The model decides whether to delegate. The harness decides what delegation is allowed to look like.

The one thing I'd add is that this only works if the model is actually good at the judgment call. Early on we saw a lot of over-spawning, where it would fan out for things that would've taken two tool calls to do inline. So some of this ended up being about the prompting and the examples you give it, and honestly just about the models getting better at knowing when a task is worth the overhead of a fresh context.

r001.rationale: The response says the model decides whether to delegate and treats spawning as a tool call, while the harness sets constraints.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the decision to delegate from the mechanics of running a subagent. The model has the task context, so it can decide, “This piece is independent enough to hand off.” The harness should expose that capability and enforce the constraints: how many agents can run, what they can access, and how their results come back.

You don’t want the harness trying to anticipate every situation where delegation is useful. But you also don’t want the model having to reinvent scheduling and lifecycle management. The model proposes the split; the harness makes it executable within a budget.

r001.rationale: The response assigns the delegation decision to the model, while the harness handles execution constraints. This locates spawning policy in the executive decision-maker.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that decision belongs in the harness, but you want the model to have a way to express when delegation would be useful. There are two different questions: “Would this task benefit from another agent?” and “Should we actually spawn one, given the resources and constraints?” The model can help with the first. The harness has to own the second, because it’s responsible for budgets, concurrency, permissions, and the lifecycle of those agents.

So I’d expose delegation as an explicit request, rather than letting every agent recursively create more agents without oversight. Then the harness can decide whether to grant it and keep track of the work and results.

r001.rationale: The response says the harness owns the decision whether to spawn agents, including whether to grant a delegation request, which places spawning policy in the harness.
